wines.head: Pinot Noir
wines.text: Oregon Pinot Noir is often called the closest in style to Burgundy. Burgundy's own leans earthy and floral. The best red Burgundy can be kept for more than 15 years.

wines.head: Chardonnay
wines.text: Oregon Chardonnay is made around bright acidity rather than a buttery feel. Willamette growers differ on Burgundy: some say their wines are growing more like white Burgundy, while others set out not to copy it.

sources.name: GuildSomm, Neal Hulkower, Willamette Valley's Way with Chardonnay

wines.head: Blends
wines.text: Red Bordeaux is usually a blend: Cabernet Sauvignon leads on the Left Bank and Merlot on the Right Bank. Many Napa wines also blend grapes, from the valley floor and the hillsides, and Inglenook, founded in 1879, was the first Bordeaux-style winery in the US.

wines.head: Taste and aging
wines.text: Wine Folly's side-by-side tasting suggests Bordeaux blends at about 12.5% alcohol, often surprisingly light, with earthy notes, and Napa ones at 14.5% or more, with much firmer tannins. Bordeaux's top Left Bank reds are concentrated and long-lived, and most are meant for the cellar.

sources.name: Wine Folly, Comparing Napa vs Bordeaux Cabernet Sauvignon

wines.head: Sauvignon Blanc
wines.text: Both are high in acidity. Sancerre is mostly bone dry, made with little oak and without malolactic fermentation, and tends to be less grassy and herbaceous than New Zealand Sauvignon Blanc. Marlborough's shows vibrant fruit and very sharp acidity, with bell pepper, gooseberry and passionfruit, and a gram or two of sugar is normal there to balance the acid.

wines.head: Tempranillo
wines.text: Tempranillo leads in both. In Ribera del Duero it is called Tinto Fino, and the hot, short growing season gives a richer style, with black cherry, blackberry and dried fig. Rioja is known for vanilla from oak, with cherry, dill and cigar box.

wines.head: Aging rules
wines.text: Both use the same aging terms and rules. A red Crianza ages at least two years, one of them in oak. A Reserva ages at least three years, one in oak. A Gran Reserva ages five years before release, two of them in oak.

wines.head: Nebbiolo
wines.text: Both are Nebbiolo from the Langhe. Barbaresco gets a slight sea influence and ripens a little earlier. Its tannins are less harsh when young and soften sooner, so it does not age as long as a traditional Barolo. Barolos from La Morra and Barolo itself come closest to Barbaresco.

wines.head: Aging rules
wines.text: Barolo must age at least three years, 18 months of them in wood, and a Riserva at least five. Barbaresco must age at least two years, 9 months in wood, and a Riserva at least four.

wines.head: Made two ways
wines.text: Champagne gets its second fermentation in the bottle, from Pinot Noir, Pinot Meunier and Chardonnay, and must age at least 15 months. Most Prosecco is made from Glera and gets its second fermentation in large steel tanks, which can take as little as 30 days.

wines.head: Taste
wines.text: Prosecco is aromatic and crisp, with yellow apple, pear, white peach and apricot, and is best drunk within three to five years of its vintage. Extra Dry is its most common style.

wines.head: Made two ways
wines.text: Cava is made like Champagne, with its second fermentation in the bottle, mostly from Macabeo, Parellada and Xarel·lo, and it spends at least 9 months on its lees. Most Prosecco is made from Glera, with its second fermentation in large steel tanks, and it needs no long aging.

wines.head: Style
wines.text: Fermenting in the bottle gives Cava fine, lasting bubbles. Prosecco is fresh and fruit-driven, with apple, pear and white peach, and Extra Dry is its most common style.

sources.name: Vinissimus, Cava, Champagne and Prosecco: differences and how to choose

wines.head: Both made in the bottle
wines.text: Both get their second fermentation in the bottle, by the traditional method. Champagne is made almost entirely from Pinot Noir, Pinot Meunier and Chardonnay. Cava is mostly Macabeo, Parellada and Xarel·lo, with Chardonnay also allowed.

wines.head: Rules
wines.text: Champagne must age at least 15 months, and vintage Champagne at least three years. Cava spends at least 9 months on its lees, and it may no longer be sold as Spanish champagne.

sources.name: Vinissimus, Cava, Champagne and Prosecco: differences and how to choose

wines.head: Blends and single grapes
wines.text: Red Bordeaux is almost always a blend, led by Cabernet Sauvignon on the Left Bank and Merlot on the Right. Red Burgundy is Pinot Noir and white Burgundy is Chardonnay. Bordeaux ranks its producers; Burgundy ranks its vineyards.

wines.head: Taste and aging
wines.text: Left Bank reds are concentrated, tannic and long-lived. Pinot Noir is usually light to medium-bodied with lower tannin, and Burgundy's leans earthy and floral. The best grand cru Burgundy can be kept for more than 15 years.

wines.head: Sherry and Port
wines.text: Sherry is made from white grapes, mostly Palomino, and fortified after fermentation, so most Sherry is dry. Port is usually a sweet red. It is fortified partway through fermentation, which leaves sugar in the wine, and it is usually 19 to 22% alcohol.

wines.head: Aging
wines.text: Sherry ages at least two years in a solera of linked barrels and does not generally improve once bottled. Ruby Port is aged only a few years. Tawny Port ages much longer in barrel, with age statements from 10 to 50 years.

wines.head: Nebbiolo and Sangiovese
wines.text: Barolo is Nebbiolo: light in color, with strong tannin, and often said to smell of tar and roses. Brunello is 100% Sangiovese, with high acidity and flavors of blackberry, black cherry, chocolate, leather and violets.

wines.head: Aging
wines.text: Barolo must age at least three years, 18 months in wood. Brunello spends two years in oak and at least four months in bottle, and is released 50 months after the harvest. Most Brunello needs at least 10 years, and traditional Barolo can take more than 10 years to soften.

wines.head: Nebbiolo and Pinot Noir
wines.text: Barolo is made from Nebbiolo. It is medium to full-bodied, with high tannin and acidity, and is often said to smell of tar and roses. Red Burgundy is mostly Pinot Noir, which is lighter and silky, with lower tannin.

wines.head: Color and age
wines.text: Both are light in color. Barolo takes on a rust-red tinge as it matures. The best red Burgundy can be kept for more than 15 years.
